summaries.example: Imagine the word “dog.” It can name an animal, but it can also fit into a sentence in a special way: “The dog runs,” or “I see the dog.” Thomas’s theory asks how a word’s meaning and its place in a sentence are connected.
summaries.summary: Thomas of Erfurt was a late medieval philosopher and grammar teacher. Very little is known about his life, but his main work, De modis significandi, was known by the early fourteenth century and became the leading textbook of a school called the Modists. Thomas thought grammar was more than a list of rules. He wanted to explain why words have meanings, why they can take different grammatical forms, and why they can join together in certain ways. The Modists connected three levels: things in the world, ideas in the mind, and words in language. Their theory was ambitious, but it became very complicated and eventually lost influence. Thomas’s book also became famous because later readers mistakenly believed it was written by Duns Scotus. That mistake brought the work to the attention of thinkers such as Charles Peirce and Martin Heidegger.
key_ideas: Thomas of Erfurt was a teacher and philosopher active in the early 1300s.
His best-known book explained grammar through the ways words can mean and combine.
He connected language with thought and with the nature of things.
His book became the main textbook for Modist grammar.
The book was later wrongly printed as if it had been written by Duns Scotus.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thomas shows that grammar can raise deep philosophical questions. When we ask how words mean, we are also asking how language relates to thinking and reality. His work helps us see that people in the Middle Ages studied language in a systematic way, not only by memorizing rules. It also teaches an important lesson about scholarship: identifying the true author of a work can change how later readers understand it.

important_terms.definition: A medieval approach to grammar that studied how words get meaning and how they fit together in sentences.
The different grammatical jobs and sentence patterns that a word can take part in.
A way of thinking about how a word, an idea, and a real thing are connected.
The joining of words in a sentence.

questions_to_think_about: Can a word have more than one job in a sentence?
Does understanding a word require knowing what it refers to?
Can we talk meaningfully about something imaginary, such as a dragon?
Why might a complicated theory eventually be replaced by a simpler one?

summaries.example: Consider the word “blindness.” It does not name a positive object in the outside world in the same way “horse” does. Thomas argues that the word can still have grammatical meaning because the mind can understand blindness positively—as the absence of sight—and language can express that concept. The word’s grammatical behavior therefore need not depend on a simple one-to-one object outside the mind.
summaries.summary: Thomas of Erfurt was the most influential member of the later medieval Modist movement, also called the speculative grammarians. His life is poorly documented, but his main treatise, De modis significandi, was circulating by about 1310 and became the movement’s standard text. Thomas treated grammar as a science whose principles should explain, rather than merely record, the forms of meaningful speech. The central principles were the modi significandi, the modes through which words signify and occupy grammatical roles. These were not isolated linguistic features. Thomas held that they arose from modi intelligendi, the mind’s modes of understanding, which in turn reflected modi essendi, the ways things are. This created a three-level account linking language, thought, and reality. The theory had resources for handling difficult examples. A word could signify a fiction such as a chimera by drawing on the imagined parts of that fiction, while a term for blindness could express a positive concept of lacking sight. Thomas also distinguished signification from reference, so grammatical analysis did not require every meaningful expression to have a corresponding external object. The Modist system eventually became too elaborate and could not adequately address context and other linguistic phenomena. Its influence nevertheless continued indirectly because the treatise was printed for centuries under Duns Scotus’s name, leading later thinkers to read Thomas through a mistaken attribution.
key_ideas: Thomas’s principal work sought a demonstrative, principle-based science of grammar rather than a merely descriptive grammar inherited from authorities such as Priscian.
The Modist account proposed a parallel structure: modes of being ground modes of understanding, which ground modes of signifying.
Thomas distinguished grammatical signification from reference, allowing his theory to discuss words for fictions and absences such as “chimera” and “blindness.”
His explanations addressed difficult cases, including grammatical forms that do not straightforwardly describe the thing named.
De modis significandi became the standard Modist text because it was relatively clear and concise, but Modism later disappeared from Paris and was replaced by other approaches.
The work’s later influence was enlarged by its mistaken attribution to Duns Scotus, affecting how Peirce and Heidegger encountered it.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thomas’s project matters because it treats grammar as a meeting point of philosophy, linguistics, and theories of mind. It asks whether the structure of language can be explained by universal principles and whether those principles reflect how humans understand the world. The entry also illustrates the importance of textual history. A mistaken attribution allowed Thomas’s ideas to enter discussions associated with Duns Scotus and shaped the way later intellectuals encountered the work. Studying the correction helps distinguish Thomas’s own theory from the interpretations built around it.

important_terms.definition: The later medieval school of speculative grammarians that explained grammar through modes of signifying, understanding, and being.
The grammatical capacities through which an expression signifies and takes roles such as noun or verb, including relevant forms of number, case, tense, or mood.
The ways the intellect understands or conceptualizes what is signified.
The properties or ways of being that things exhibit outside the mind and that, in the Modist theory, ground understanding.
The philosophical study of meaning or signification, distinguished in the entry from reference.
The relation by which an expression is connected to what it stands for; the entry treats this as a matter for logic rather than grammar alone.
The proper joining of words into constructions and the formation of grammatically complete expressions.
A work explaining grammar through principles rather than merely reporting traditional grammatical rules.

questions_to_think_about: Should a theory of grammar explain only sentence structure, or also the nature of meaning and thought?
Does a word need a real object outside the mind in order to have meaning?
What is gained and what is lost when grammar is modeled on a general theory of reality?
Could a theory that ignores context explain how speakers communicate imperfect or unusual sentences?
When does adding explanations to save a theory make the theory too complicated to be useful?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “The dragon is sleeping.” There may be no real dragon, but the sentence still has a familiar grammatical shape. Thomas’s approach can explain this by saying that the word “dragon” has a meaning based on an imagined creature and its imagined features. Grammar and meaning do not depend only on whether the named thing exists outside the mind.
summaries.summary: Thomas of Erfurt was a medieval philosopher and teacher associated with the Modists, a group interested in the deep structure of language. Almost nothing certain is known about his life. His most important work was De modis significandi, a treatise on grammar that became the standard Modist textbook. Thomas believed that grammar should be explained through principles. The key idea was that words have “modes of signifying”: patterns that help determine what grammatical jobs they can perform and how they can combine with other words. He connected these modes with two further levels. Modes of understanding describe how the mind forms concepts, while modes of being describe properties found in things. Thus, the Modists proposed a relationship among words, thoughts, and reality. This theory was meant to explain why different parts of speech and sentence patterns exist. It also tried to handle challenging cases. Words can refer to imagined things, such as chimeras, and to absences, such as blindness, even though these are not ordinary positive objects outside the mind. Thomas’s book was widely copied and printed, but Modism later disappeared as other methods of studying logic and language became more persuasive. Its historical influence increased because it was mistakenly treated as a work by Duns Scotus. Peirce and Heidegger therefore encountered Thomas’s ideas while believing, at least for a time, that they belonged to Scotus.
key_ideas: Thomas wanted grammar to have reasons and principles, not just rules handed down by earlier teachers.
He connected language to both human thought and the properties of things.
His theory could discuss words for imaginary things and for absences, not only ordinary physical objects.
His main book became the most important textbook of the Modist tradition.
Modism declined partly because its explanations became very complex and did not handle context well.
Later scholars first knew the book through an incorrect attribution to Duns Scotus.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thomas’s work matters because it shows that questions about grammar can also be questions about knowledge and reality. His theory asks whether the patterns of language reflect patterns in thought and in the world. It also provides a useful example of how intellectual traditions change: a theory may become influential, face serious problems, and still affect later thinkers. Finally, the story of the mistaken attribution shows why historians compare manuscripts and investigate who really wrote a text.

important_terms.definition: A group of later medieval thinkers who studied grammar as a systematic theory of how words signify and combine.
The ways a word can signify and function in language, including its possible grammatical roles and forms.
The ways a person’s mind understands or forms concepts about things.
The ways a thing can be or the properties it can have in reality.
The study of meaning, especially how words and expressions signify.
The way words are arranged and connected to form phrases and sentences.

questions_to_think_about: Can an imaginary word still have meaning? Why?
How might the way we think affect the way we use grammar?
Is a complicated explanation better than a simple one if it explains more cases?
Why could ignoring context make it hard to explain communication?
How might a mistaken author’s name change the history of a book?
